source_text: Sed quod supra intermisimus ex parte subsecutae disputationis, ne cohaerentiam eius dispergeremus, nunc responso expungemus. Ubi enim gradum fiximus de apostoli absoluta definitione, omnem mulierem etiam omnis aetatis intellegendam, responderi ex diverso habebat ergo a nativitate et a primo nomine aetatis virginem operiri oportere. Non ita est autem, sed ex quo se intellegere coeperit et sensum naturae suae intrare et de virginis exire et pati novum illud quod alterius aetatis est. Nam et principes generis Adam et Eva, quamdiu intellectu carebant, nudi agebant. At ubi de arbore agnitionis gustaverunt, nihil primum senserunt quam erubescendum. Ita sui quique sexus intellectum tegmine notaverunt. Sed etsi propter angelos velanda est, sine dubio ab ea aetate lex velaminis operabitur a qua potuerunt filiae hominum concupiscentiam sui adducere et nuptias pati. Ex illo enim virgo desinit ex quo potest non esse. Et ideo penes Israël illicitum est ad virum tradere nisi post contestatam sanguine maturitatem; ita ante hunc indicem acerba res est. Igitur si tam diu virgo quamdiu acerba est, desinit virginem eum matura cognoscitur, et ut non virgo iam legi applicatur, sicut et nuptiis. Et desponsatae quidem habent exemplum Rebeccae, quae cum ad sponsum ignotum adhuc ignota perduceretur, simul ipsum cognovit esse quem de longinquo prospexerat, non sustinuit dexterae colluctationem nec osculi congressionem nec salutationis communicationem, sed confessa quod senserat, id est spiritu nuptam, negavit virginem velata ibidem. O mulierem iam de Christi disciplina! Ostendit enim etiam nuptias de aspectu et animo fieri, quemadmodum stuprum; nisi quod etiam Rebeccam quidam adhuc velant. De ceteris vero, id est quae desponsatae non sunt, viderit parentum procrastinatio ex angustiis vel scrupulositate descendens, viderit et ipsum continentiae votum. Nihil pertinet ad aetatem sua spatia currentem suaque debita maturitati luentem. Alia in occulto mater, natura, et alius in latenti pater, tempus, filiam suam legibus suis maritarunt. Aspice nuptam iam illam tuam virginem, et animam expectatione et carnem transfiguratione, cui tu secundum paras maritum. Iam et vox obsolefacta est, et membra completa sunt, et pudor ubique vestitur, et menses tributa dependunt, ac tu mulierem negas quam muliebria pati dicis? Si congressio viri mulierem facit, non tegantur nisi post ipsam nuptiarum passionem. Atquin etiam apud ethnicos velatae ad virum ducuntur. Si autem ad desponsationem velantur, quia et corpore et spiritu masculo mixtae sunt per osculum et dexteras, per quae primum resignarunt pudorem spiritu, per commune conscientiae pignus quo totam condixerunt confusionem, quanto magis tempus illas velabit, sine quo sponsari non possunt et quo urgente sine sponsalibus virgines desinunt esse? Tempus etiam ethnici observant, ut ex lege naturae iura sua aetatibus reddant. Nam feminas quidem a duodecim annis, masculum vero a duobus amplius ad negotia mittunt, pubertatem in annis, non sponsalibus aut nuptiis decernentes. Mater familiae vocatur, licet virgo, et pater familiae, licet investis. A nobis nec naturalia observantur, quasi alius sit deus naturae quam noster.
thought_title: Maturity, not birth, begins the obligation of the veil
orientation: Tertullian is answering an objection to his earlier argument that the apostle's word 'woman' includes every age, and he now explains that the veil becomes obligatory when a girl reaches the age of self-understanding and sexual maturity.
pass_a_gloss: But what we passed over above, from part of the following discussion, so that we would not scatter its coherence, we will now discharge with a response. For where we fixed the step from the apostle's absolute definition, that every woman of every age is to be understood, it had to be answered from the other side: therefore a virgin ought to be veiled from birth and from the first name of age. But it is not so, but from when she has begun to understand herself and to enter into the feeling of her own nature and to go out from the state of a virgin and to suffer that new thing which belongs to another age. For also the first parents of the race, Adam and Eve, as long as they lacked understanding, went about naked. But when they tasted from the tree of knowledge, they felt nothing first except that they must be ashamed. Thus each marked the understanding of their own sex with a covering. But even if she must be veiled because of the angels, without doubt the law of the veil will be in force from that age from which the daughters of men were able to draw to themselves desire for themselves and to undergo marriage. For from that point a virgin ceases to be, from which she is able not to be one. And therefore among Israel it is unlawful to hand over to a man except after maturity attested by blood; thus before this sign the matter is unripe. Therefore if she is a virgin as long as she is unripe, she ceases to be a virgin when she is recognized as mature, and as no longer a virgin she is now subject to the law, just as also to marriage. And the betrothed indeed have the example of Rebecca, who, when she was being led to a bridegroom unknown to her while she was still unknown, as soon as she recognized that he was the one whom she had seen from afar, she did not endure the clasping of the right hand nor the meeting of a kiss nor the sharing of a greeting, but confessing what she had felt, that is, that she was married in spirit, she denied that she was a virgin by veiling herself on the spot. O woman already of the discipline of Christ! For she showed that even marriages come about from sight and mind, just as fornication does; except that some still veil even Rebecca. But concerning the rest, that is, those who are not betrothed, let the parents' delay, descending from difficulties or scrupulosity, see to it, and let the vow of continence itself see to it. Nothing pertains to age, which runs through its own spaces and pays its own debts to maturity. Another mother in secret, nature, and another father in hiding, time, have married their daughter by their own laws. Look at that virgin of yours already married, both in soul by expectation and in flesh by transformation, for whom you are preparing a husband according to your own schedule. Already her voice has become worn, and her limbs have become full, and modesty is clothed everywhere, and her months pay their tribute, and do you deny that she is a woman, when you say she suffers the things of women? If intercourse with a man makes a woman, let them not be veiled except after the very suffering of marriage. But indeed even among the heathen they are veiled when they are led to a man. But if they are veiled at betrothal, because they have been mingled with a male both in body and in spirit through the kiss and the right hands, through which they first unsealed their modesty in spirit, through the common pledge of conscience by which they agreed to the whole confusion, how much more will time veil them, without which they cannot be betrothed, and by whose pressure virgins cease to be virgins even without betrothals? Time even the heathen observe, so that by the law of nature they render their own rights to ages. For they send females indeed from twelve years, but the male from two years more, to business, determining puberty by years, not by betrothals or marriages. She is called mother of a family, although a virgin, and he father of a family, although not yet clothed with the toga. Among us not even natural things are observed, as if the God of nature were other than ours.

lemmas.gloss: we fixed the step, established the point

choices.english: from when she has begun to understand herself
choices.why: Keeps the reflexive force of 'se' and the inceptive aspect of 'coeperit', marking the start of self-awareness as the trigger for veiling.
rejected: from the time she begins to know herself

choices.term: pati novum illud quod alterius aetatis est
choices.english: to suffer that new thing which belongs to another age
choices.why: Preserves 'pati' as 'suffer' to convey the passive experience of puberty, and 'alterius aetatis' as 'another age' to keep the contrast with her previous state.
rejected: to experience that new thing of another stage of life
to undergo that novelty of a different age

choices.english: they felt nothing first except that they must be ashamed
choices.why: Renders the gerundive 'erubescendum' as an obligation ('must be ashamed'), matching the Latin impersonal necessity.
rejected: they first felt nothing but shame
they perceived nothing before that they should blush

choices.why: Keeps the legal-ritual force of 'contestatam' (attested, confirmed) and the concrete 'sanguine' (by blood), preserving the reference to menstruation as proof of maturity.

choices.english: she denied that she was a virgin by veiling herself on the spot
choices.why: Keeps 'negavit' as 'denied' with the infinitive, and 'ibidem' as 'on the spot' to emphasize the immediacy of Rebecca's action.
rejected: she refused to be a virgin, veiling herself there
she disowned her virginity by veiling at once

choices.why: Preserves the metaphor of 'tributa dependunt' (pay tribute) for menstruation, keeping the economic-legal image Tertullian uses.
rejected: her monthly periods pay their dues

bible_refs.note: Adam and Eve, after eating from the tree of knowledge, knew they were naked and made coverings; Tertullian paraphrases 'nudi agebant... nihil primum senserunt quam erubescendum'.
Rebecca saw Isaac from afar, took her veil, and covered herself; Tertullian retells this as 'non sustinuit dexterae colluctationem... negavit virginem velata ibidem'.

pass_b_english: But let me now settle the point I passed over earlier, so as not to break the thread of the argument. When I established from the apostle's absolute definition that every woman of every age must be understood, the objection from the other side was that a virgin would then have to be veiled from birth and from the first name of her age. But that is not how it is. She must be veiled from the time she begins to understand herself, to enter into the awareness of her own nature, to leave the state of virginity, and to suffer that new thing which belongs to another age. For Adam and Eve, the first parents of our race, went about naked as long as they lacked understanding. But when they tasted from the tree of knowledge, the first thing they felt was that they must be ashamed, and so each marked the understanding of their own sex with a covering.

But even if a woman must be veiled because of the angels, the law of the veil will without doubt take effect from the age at which the daughters of men could draw desire to themselves and undergo marriage. For a virgin ceases to be a virgin from the moment she is able not to be one. That is why among Israel it is unlawful to hand a girl over to a man until her maturity has been attested by blood; before that sign she is considered unripe. So if she is a virgin as long as she is unripe, she ceases to be a virgin when she is recognized as mature, and since she is no longer a virgin she is subject to the law, just as she is to marriage.

Betrothed women have the example of Rebecca. When she was being led to a bridegroom still unknown to her, herself still unknown to him, the moment she recognized that he was the one she had seen from afar, she did not endure the clasping of his right hand, nor the meeting of a kiss, nor the sharing of a greeting. Instead she confessed what she had felt—that she was already a bride in spirit—and by veiling herself on the spot she denied that she was a virgin. What a woman already instructed in the discipline of Christ! She showed that even marriage happens through sight and mind, just as adultery does—except that some people still veil Rebecca herself.

As for the rest, those who are not betrothed, let the parents' delay, born of narrow circumstances or scrupulosity, be their concern; let the vow of continence itself be their concern. None of this has anything to do with age, which runs its own course and pays its own debts to maturity. Another mother in secret, nature, and another father in hiding, time, have married their daughter by their own laws. Look at that virgin of yours: she is already married—her soul by expectation, her flesh by transformation—for whom you are preparing a second husband. Her voice has already deepened, her limbs have filled out, modesty clothes her everywhere, her months pay their tribute—and you deny that she is a woman, when you admit she suffers a woman's things?

If union with a man makes a woman, then let no one be veiled until after the actual experience of marriage. But even among the pagans, women are veiled when they are led to their husbands. If they are veiled at betrothal, because they have been joined to a male in body and spirit through the kiss and the right hands—through which they first unsealed their modesty in spirit, through the common pledge of conscience by which they pledged all their shame—how much more will time veil them, without which they cannot be betrothed, and under whose pressure virgins cease to be virgins even without betrothal?

Even the pagans observe time, so that by the law of nature they render to each age its own rights. They send girls out to business at twelve years old, and boys two years later, determining puberty by years, not by betrothals or marriages. A girl is called mother of a family, even if she is a virgin; a boy is called father of a family, even if he is still beardless. Among us not even the natural things are observed, as if the God of nature were different from ours.

problems.quote: and you are preparing a husband for her as if she were still a second self
problems.why: 'secundum' means 'in accordance with' (the law), not 'as if a second self'. The sense is: you prepare a husband for her according to [the law].
problems.fix: for whom you prepare a husband according to the law
problems.ruling: Source ‘cui tu secundum paras maritum’ uses ‘secundum’ = ‘according to’, not ‘as if a second self’

problems.quote: through the common pledge of conscience by which they agreed to complete mutual shame
problems.source_quote: per commune conscientiae pignus quo totam condixerunt confusionem
problems.why: 'condixerunt' means 'agreed upon' or 'settled'; 'totam confusionem' = 'all their shame/modesty'. 'Complete mutual shame' misrepresents the object as reciprocal rather than total.
problems.fix: through the common pledge of conscience by which they pledged all their shame
problems.ruling: Source ‘per commune conscientiae pignus quo totam condixerunt confusionem’ means ‘by which they settled the whole confusion’, not ‘complete mutual shame’

problems.quote: even if he is still unbearded
problems.fix: even if he is still invested (clothed).
problems.ruling: 'investis' means unclothed/unvested, not unbearded; contrast with virgin mother-of-family requires male not yet invested, not beardless.

fixed: Corrected 'as if she were still a second self' to 'according to the law' (source: 'cui tu secundum paras maritum').
Corrected 'complete mutual shame' to 'all their shame' (source: 'totam condixerunt confusionem').

problems.quote: for whom you are preparing a husband according to the law
problems.why: "secundum" here means "a second" husband, since nature and time have already married her. The English wrongly reads it as the preposition "according to", which loses the point.
problems.fix: for whom you are preparing a second husband.

problems.quote: even if he is still invested
problems.why: "investis" means beardless or immature, not yet grown. "Invested" is a false friend and makes no sense to a reader.
problems.fix: even if he is still beardless.

fixed: cui tu secundum paras maritum: secundum cannot be prepositional with no object and agrees with maritum; nature/time already married her, so yours is a second husband.
licet investis: investis means beardless/not yet grown, not invested; fixed false friend.

last_rejected.why: 'a duobus amplius' means 'from two years onward' (i.e., from age two-plus), not 'two years later' after twelve.
last_rejected.fix: and boys from two years onward
last_rejected.ruling: "a duobus amplius" means ‘by two more (years)’ after the girls’ twelve, i.e., boys sent two years later, not from age two.

last_rejected.quote: But let me now settle the point I passed over earlier, so as not to break the thread of the argument.
last_rejected.source_quote: Sed quod supra intermisimus ex parte subsecutae disputationis, ne cohaerentiam eius dispergeremus, nunc responso expungemus.
last_rejected.why: The purpose clause explains the earlier omission, made for the discussion that followed, not the present reply.
last_rejected.fix: But what I passed over above for the sake of the discussion that followed, lest I break its thread, I will now settle in reply.
last_rejected.ruling: 'ne cohaerentiam eius dispergeremus' is ambiguous in English. The sense stays close: not breaking the argument's thread explains the delay either way. This is a minor attachment issue, not a changed meaning.

last_rejected.quote: to leave the state of virginity
last_rejected.why: Genitive virginis means leaving the virgin's age, parallel to the next age, not ceasing to be a virgin.
last_rejected.fix: to pass out of the virgin's age
last_rejected.ruling: 'de virginis exire' means leaving the virgin's condition. 'State of virginity' is within range, and the next clause's 'alterius aetatis' supports it. Meaning is not changed.
